segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: It's the regular play button. You see this one regular button here? And the record button. You can touch them both at once. And you can see it through recording. See this little needle right there?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Okay, when you talk it bounces. Uh huh. Okay.

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Okay.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, I'd like to talk about your grandfather. He said that he was, he, he home set out there, or he bought a place out there in the Avon area?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, no, he didn't buy a place. He took up some land, and my aunt had taken, took up a 40, and the place he took, what they call a preemption, he bought it and he filed on part of it, and part of it he paid cash for. And they called that a preemption. Right. Before he bought it. And he did lots of hard work on that place. And when he stopped them, they was never going to get any returns out of it. When the W &I and railroad, W &I and M railroad built through, they helped out a good deal.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, did they build through his property?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Yes, they did. So close to it that they had to pay him a little right of way, a couple of bonds or a right of way, where it crossed. I remember I'd get all this stuff mixed up in my days, so much of it I listened to when I was around my grandfather's home, where I lived for quite a while. So I'd go out huckleberrying on daytime, I'd listen to them talk in the evening. I'd lose track of things. And the one last year that had just huckleberried, I dressed in men's clothes and took to those, took my lunch in a little bucket of water, and took to the particular place that I moved. And I stayed with it, and I didn't tell anybody where it was, either, until I picked 45 gallons and sold them.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How much were huckleberries selling for, then?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: About a dollar a gallon. That's about all you could get. All you dared ask them to sell them at all is, you're not apt to lose your people who was buying the berries. You're not going to ask them much. But it was a pretty good price. Anyway, I got 45 gallons out of that deal, and I was selfish, and I kept the, where I bought the, the, the, the pats, too. Maybe you've heard of Cedar Gulch. Well, because in Cedar Gulch, most of Cedar Gulch is where I was picking those berries. I didn't care to go in too far because there was no cougars around that place. I saw her once, and I saw her once or twice. But I am not much of a coward. I'm not afraid of coyotes at all. Cougars, I guess I would say, so long as you keep your distance from them. They generally take one good look at you and go sneaking off. I just got one of those carried up in the woods that I didn't have anybody with me, a gun or anything else. I didn't have any protection, but I had some pretty swift feet as soon as they got, the cougar got out of sight, I did too.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: The cougar never gave you any trouble then?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: You could hear him sometimes at night, groaning or yelling. I think there was more than one in the last trip of woods. I think there was a pair, is what I think. At night, they sometimes say, yell, back and forth. They had kind of a scary sounding yell. Excuse my echoes. But that's what I get. I don't get to talking too much.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Were there bears up in that huckleberry patch, too?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, there was lots of huckleberry patches in them, but they're kind of frozen out now. These last two or three big heavy with frost in them, they come and set them back up. Some of the neighbors said they didn't find out about any good birds last year at all. Then it kind of goes by, they get them one year, then maybe two or three years before they get good ones again. I didn't get a chance to go to look much for them a second time. The cougar had been seen two or three times. I was getting kind of wary. I didn't want to hang around up in there. More afraid of the cougar than there was of the bears. I saw bears there all the time. It didn't scare me.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What did the neighbors think of you getting dressed up in men's clothes and going out to go huckleberry?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, about the usual thing. They was sorry for themselves because I didn't ask them to go to huckleberry. I saw a man say, well, there's some of them I didn't face at all. Some of them, of course, are kind of a lot of stregandous here. A lady is supposed to be a lady dressed in a men's clothes, but I don't know whose business it was. So, I told her there were three different ones that I didn't see her in clothes. She said, oh, don't you hate to dress in men's clothes once it's safe? I said, well, I'm safe then. Well, there's no heavy illness. If I want to dress in men's clothes, then... Right. And I was... I was grown up. I was an old maid. I was too old to be even when I wasn't an old maid. I was picking the huckleberry.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: This is before you were married, though, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, yes… but I'd known my husband ever since we were kids. We went to school together. He was only a couple of years older than I was. His folks lived there, and he took them to place. And we went to school after. Last time we were quit, but he didn't go to school. So we died. And we got a claim.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How did your husband go about courting you?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, he could just come to see me. We saw each other pretty... When we was going to school, we saw each other every day. He didn't... when he froze on. He knew what he wanted, and what he wanted. He wanted to be his best girl. He would come and work for my grandfather sometimes. And his mother kind of engineered things. She wanted me for a daughter-in-law, and she kind of engineered things around. She was kind of pushy lady, not very well, but of a good nature and good hearted. And his father was an Englishman, and he was off of good hearted. And I've got a picture of him. It's over in that dresser drawer. A big picture of him taking side by side. But she wasn't very well. And he wasn't as... Mr. Thurtle wasn't as well as they thought he was, come to find out. And my husband had cancer. He found out the fact. He didn't complain very much until right after last. Said he didn't feel very good. And there was no hand to complain of his or his. He told me he was watching out for mine. Not asking if he didn't feel very good. He didn't feel very good, he asked. I told him we'd better make an agreement. About our tempers, because we both had tempers. I said, let's make an agreement. When we get up in the morning and you feel cross, I'll try and keep still. And when I feel cross, you try and keep still. And I said, between the two of us maybe we won't fight. He laughed. But he was no hand to quarrel. Anyway, but when he said things, and meant them, he didn't want them to get out of his way. Any of the neighbors, he wouldn't. He always got along with them after a fashion. But they never wanted to leave him alone. Pretty well. Because he was a big fella. He was over 6 foot tall. When he was feeling well, he weighed about 2560 or 60, about 6 foot tall. He was a pretty big man. He didn't feel much like a father. He used to get after me when I tried to drive a team for him when we was hauling in hay. He said, you drive horses the funniest way. Well, I said, to go?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: He said, yes, but if you can make them go the way I do, it'll save you lots of trouble. Well, I said, if it gets us to where we want to go and get some hay, what's the difference? He had three horses. He had a third horse that came in for the end. It also came in for the ending for the neighbors.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was there a lot of loaning and borrowing stuff with the neighbors?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, quite a bit. That's the way they did it in that neighborhood. It's all like I told Frank, I said, I don't mind the borrow. I said, don't forget to bring it back. That's what... I didn't bother. But they're all pretty good about bringing it back.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: After you were married, you farmed then? You and your husband did farming after you were married?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, yes. We met when I was 12 when he was 14. That's when we met in the 20th horse mode in the neighborhood up there. They didn't get around to much farming for quite a little while, but they finally did have a nice little place there. Done pretty well with it, too. There's a farm already. They're both hard workers. I've got a picture of them.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: That's okay. I can look at it later.

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: I probably won't think of it at the end.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: I'll think of it later. That's all right.

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: It's over in the top of one of those drawers.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did he come straight over to Idaho from England?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: My grandfather came from England. English blood, too, but he came from Iowa straight over. Mr. Thurtle, he had lived in Wisconsin, I guess, someplace like that in the east. When he decided to move, he came over to the place.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How many kids were there in your school when you went to school there in Avon?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, in Avon there was quite a few. I don't know exactly how many. I know sometimes she had quite a... More little kids than big kids. She had mixture of old. She had several classes of older children. I don't remember.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did the teacher usually have a pretty easy time keeping the kids in line, or did the kids get out of line a lot?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: She had a pretty easy time because they didn't do any dirty work. They minded when the kid was under her care in school. They minded, earned the mind, what they were spoken to.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How would she discipline some of the bigger boys who might be bigger than she was?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: They wouldn't do anything to make her discipline. She just talked to them. She could get them that way. She had a fairly good school. They weren't very restrictive. There weren't very many big boys, grown-up boys. Those that were away, she was just telling them, you're grown up, you don't act like a little kid. She was just talking. Some of the little ones had to be a little disciplined. They had a mother. When she spoke to them, they said, you're going to be all right.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, your mother was a school teacher?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Yes.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, I see.

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: My mother was a teacher.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was that kind of hard for you to be going to school where your mother was teaching?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, I went to school some of the time. She was very much teaching. She had to board me with somebody near the school. Then, because I was young and couldn't walk so far, she had to, from her own home, she had about two and a half, three miles to walk. So she boarded with a lady, with someone, people she knew. She'd board with them from Monday to, well, from, of course, Monday night, Monday evening, and the story was separate, and then Friday morning, Friday would be another day, and the Saturday and Sunday in between didn't count. And against her.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, so she would board in town and you would walk to school from your grandparents' place? She, from where? She would board in town, and then would you walk to school from your grandparents' place?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, no, I wasn't big enough to. And, see, she taught school a little bit before I was old enough to go to school. She'd leave me home with my grandmother and teach school. And I had orders to mind what Grandma said, too. She hated to do that because my grandmother did all the work pretty hard, and she said, there's too much work for her. My grandmother told me, I'd worry about that. But it really was hard on her because she was right age, and she should have had work a lot easier. Her kids were going up, and the grandkids were pissed, I guess. She always claimed that they knew her, but I know kids now. My cousin, my cousin, it was just the two of us for a while, and he was about 15 months younger than I. And, of course, I bossed him.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: You what?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: I bossed him. I was the oldest of the two grandchildren, so I was boss. Well, he was the first one to be boss, by me. As long as there was others, it was all right.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of things would you do as a kid to amuse yourselves?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: We would play. We'd have to play pretty much. And then we had dogs, cats, chickens, geese, gate bells. The guinea fellas are the same as the nymphs, but I could take the hawks away. Scare them a little bit, and they'd play at the top of the barn, and yell until the hawks decided it was time to get out. There's a white bus, and a red one, too, on the red car, too. Two red ones. Someone would get my home and school, I guess.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, how long did you live with your grandparents? How long did you live with your grandparents?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Until I was still living with them. I was pretty well grown myself. And then the home was them, but I was supposed to help with the work. I helped my grandmother with the work. My aunt that taught school, she was home during vacation time, and she did outside work. She didn't make it to the house.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was most of the work you did housework?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Huh?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was most of the work you did housework?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: It would be housework, mostly, until my grandfather got to keep quite a bit of stock. And then we had, she had more of a house to do than she'd buy the geese and the pigs and the things like that. And my grandfather's neck room for them on his place. She'd buy the feed for them, the fat ones, and we'd have all the pork we wanted, some to sell to everyone, and some beef. My grandfather always made? Well, always tried to buy a quarter of a beef in the fall, so they had us, some of us sold it down, more dry beef made for winter. We had it made where we'd like to get in the best of anybody. He had to go somewhere to get the best of my grandfather. My grandfather would tell them where to head in. Ha ha ha ha.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Your grandfather was a pretty sharp trader?

segments.speaker: Alics Thurtle
segments.words: Huh?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was your grandfather a pretty sharp trader?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, sharp enough so he didn't lose much when he was trading. He didn't go in for being such a sharp trader. He'd been raised in, he'd been in Iowa for a long time before he came out. He went outside and he tried to raise fields of grain along in a hark town and sell it. So much. My grandmother had to hire a girl to stay with her while my grandfather was gone. And then he began to lose out kinda in that kind of business and got a chance to come out west. So he thought maybe he'd do better out here so he came. And he did pretty well. My uncle's helping.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did he have to clear the timber off the land when he came to Avon?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, no. He could sell the timber to the Potlatch. Sell of it and he would have to handle it. The Potlatch would handle it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would Potlatch pull stumps too or was it, were there still stumps in the field?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, they wouldn't pull the stumps so much but they'd get to cut the logs on the ship from the outside. There goes a green car. You got every color in the last thing you had to go. Told her it was a pretty hard life all the way around. I don't know what that man was doing.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Um, how old were you when you married your husband?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Huh?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How old were you when you married your husband?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, we were both pretty old. Let's see, I was, I was twenty-eight.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, that's not too old.

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Too old or no… he was just only a couple of years older than I.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did people get married a lot younger those days usually than they do now?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, sometimes they do. Sometimes they don't. Just depends on the people. I had one boy that was a... What do we call him? Now there's more than that. No, I got some sick and tired of him. I didn't know what to do. I used to hate but he was very well into me.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What did he do that made you sick and tired of him?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, just... I wasn't in love with the man. I didn't want to marry him. I didn't want him hanging around. And he couldn't take a hint. I never saw such a dummy. He wanted to get married so bad that he couldn't see. He didn't see a hint of a big print. I come right out and told him what I thought and made him mad. I wasn't bothered with the boys very much in school.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: After you got married, did you move to your own place and start working on your own place? Or did you stay with the Thurtles over here?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Not his place. He had a place. Oh, he had his own place at that time.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Had he bought that or homesteaded himself?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, I don't remember now just how I wrote it. He lived there. His father had that to get the place to start with. Then after his father got sold, he couldn't run it anymore. In fact, I was able to run it. So it was kind of his place then. They considered it his place.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did he farm very much land there?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Huh?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did he farm very much land?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: No, not very very much. It was 88 acres. I think he sold all the jobs altogether. 88 acres on a little piece of timber land. He had a good spring, right at his front door. His native water is irony. Some people don't like it because it tastes so strong of iron. But it's good water. People are not very well. No. My eyes say jazz watching a car go by on that thing.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was it pretty easy to support yourself off a small piece like an 80 acre?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Well, there was only one man to do the work. Well, you don't want too big a place because they can't do it. Because lots of times they can't hire because then they lose the neighborhood. They're working for other people. Here comes the white bus. And the green car. Oh, string on it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Didn't he have to hire help around haying time?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, yes the neighbors helped each other. Then lots of times there was somebody traveling through it who wanted a few days work. And then that Potlatch got busy. There was, why there was, then going back and forth. Then it worked in the camps and quit. It was quite a circulation.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did your husband never work for Potlatch?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Huh?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did your husband never work for Potlatch?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Yes, he worked for Potlatch.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What did he do?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, he worked for the ranch. He sold grain to them. He liked them. And he worked in those.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was he selling grain for their horse teams?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Huh?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was he selling grain to them for their horse teams?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Yeah. He had a team for seed for the next year. He had three horses.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What were their names?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: One, if I can remember. Beauty was one. She was kind of pretty. And then, then, she was... What did he call them? I'm trying to think what he called them. The other two horses. He had them names, I can't think right now. Just exactly what they were. They changed their names every once in a while.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Were you decided they were differently thought or something?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, no. Just didn't do most anything to pass time away. Maybe up in the woods like that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What would you do to pass time?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, yeah, we had parties. Shivarees. Shivarees.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What's a shivaree?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: That's when a couple get married and the crowd moves in and has a good time.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What would they do?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, play games and congratulate each other.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Is a shivaree kind of a surprise thing that people do?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Shivaree. All those that got married, they'd fully expect that they had a shivaree. And be disappointed if they didn't. They'd go get a gang of young folks together, you know, and take something to eat, and they'd go move in on these people that had just been married. If they were living at the folks' home, they'd move in on them and they'd have a good time playing games and so forth.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: They'd play tricks on the people and stuff, too? They'd play tricks on the people that got married and stuff, too?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Yeah… even when they pick up.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of games and what kind of tricks would they do?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, games. Kind of the Virgin Woman. Dancing and doing kind of... I never danced in my family, but then, plus, I was a dead. They'd skip the move, and you'd probably have heard that. My brain is getting stirred up so much, I wouldn't know it at all. Pretty soon. Trying to think of any different games. I kind of left. I guess I might have to get to... When you get to 83, you think you've done better than you're sure. I'm thinking.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What other things… when there wasn't somebody getting married, that you could go shivaree them. What else would you do to amuse yourselves?

segments.speaker: Alice Thurtle
segments.words: Oh, just playing parties. I'd bake up some cake and make sandwiches and go to somebody's house, and then just play these games that are like shivaree. They're good to own. They're literary, if you ever heard of that. Uh-huh. You played different games. Until they got tired, and then they'd eat their sandwiches. Tell everybody goodnight and leave. Put your dress down. She's only 79 years old, and she does this. What... See if I can get her to keep her clothes down, then.
